implementation_notes: The structure is expressible: a trait with one method per product kind returning Box<dyn AbstractProduct>, implemented by a unit struct per family. But factory traits are rarely the idiomatic Rust answer - object safety rules out generic factory methods (E0038), each product pays a heap allocation, and the community prefers generics (static dispatch, no allocation) or an enum of families with match dispatch for closed family sets. Choose the dyn form only when families are genuinely open at runtime (plugins); otherwise enum dispatch or generics express the same family-consistency intent with better performance and exhaustive checks.
pitfalls: Object safety: one generic method on the factory trait makes it unusable as dyn (E0038), which is the most common dead end when porting the pattern to Rust.
Box<dyn Trait> erases concrete types and allocates per product; hot-path creation should use generics or enums.
Trait objects with associated types need explicit bindings (Box<dyn Factory<Output = T>>), so associated-type factories rarely survive as trait objects.
Object safety: one generic method on the factory trait makes it unusable as dyn (E0038), so keep runtime-selected factory methods object-safe.
Trait objects with associated types need explicit bindings and often a type-erasing wrapper, so associated-type factories rarely survive as trait objects unchanged.
The dyn form requires heap allocation; if the family set is known at compile time, a generic with PhantomData<F> or enum dispatch avoids that allocation.
A wildcard match arm can map an unknown product kind to a valid-looking product from the wrong family or kind; return a Result and reject unknown keys explicitly.

variants.name: Enum of families with match dispatch
variants.idiom_name: enum Theme { Dark, Light } + match arms returning product enums
variants.implementation_notes: When the family set is closed, an enum of families (or of products) with match arms is the idiomatic Rust factory: no vtable, no allocation, exhaustive matching, and the compiler rejects a match that misses a family. Products can be enums too, which keeps everything inline and Copy-able; the cost is that adding a family touches the enum and every match, and open plugin systems cannot express families as new enum variants at runtime.
pitfalls: The family set becomes closed: runtime-loaded families cannot add enum variants, so plugins still need dyn.
Match arms multiply as families x product kinds; a missing arm is caught by the compiler only if there is no wildcard fallback.
Product enums grow large and every consumer match must be updated when a product kind is added.
